content: Tobacco is tropical in origin but grown under tropical, sub-tropical, and temperate climates from coast-line to 3,000 feet altitude. It requires about 100 to 120 days frost-free climate with an average temperature of 80°F to mature, liberal and well-distributed monthly rainfall of 88 to 125 mm, and relative humidity of 70-80% in the morning to 50-60% at midday. Major climatic factors influencing growth, flowering, and metabolism are rainfall, temperature, relative humidity, wind, and sunlight.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Ideal rainfall distribution for best yield and quality consists of: cloudy weather with drizzling soon after transplanting; light rainfall in the early growth stage; bright sunshine with occasional moderate rain in the grand growth period; and no rain at all during ripening (maturity) of leaves, as rain washes away gums from leaf surfaces resulting in poor curing.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Tobacco requires considerable water for leaf turgidity and expansion but is very sensitive to flooded or waterlogged soil conditions due to oxygen deprivation in soil, which is essential for fibrous and vigorous root system development. Heavy clayey soils are ruled out for monsoon cultivation due to inundation risks.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In Andhra Pradesh, annual South-West monsoon rainfall is 800-1000 mm (June to October). FCV tobacco is raised in the rabi season from October-November to February-March when temperatures are suitable, grown on conserved moisture in black soils, under irrigation in Northern Light soils, or with North-East monsoon cyclonic rains in Prakasam and Nellore districts. The crop requires good sunlight, low evaporation, high relative humidity, sustained soil moisture, and freedom from wet footing and cyclonic storms.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In Mysore district, Karnataka, average annual rainfall is 650 to 1000 mm, with over 80% received during the south-west monsoon (May to October) coinciding with the FCV crop season. Mean minimum temperature is around 15°C in January and 34°C in April. Lower diurnal temperatures, higher relative humidity, and monsoonic rains during May to September provide ideal climatic conditions for producing high-quality flue-cured tobacco.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In North Bengal, Motihari and Jati tobaccos grow in humid and damp weather throughout the year. Day temperature ranges from 5°C in December-January to 35°C in April-May. Average annual precipitation exceeds 3000 mm (mostly June-August). Relative humidity is around 85% during April and May, facilitating easy handling and conditioning of cured leaf.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In North Bihar, warm and humid weather during the second fortnight of October favors transplant establishment. Low temperature, bright sunshine, and low humidity during early growth promote thick, heavy-bodied leaves. In Tamil Nadu, chewing tobacco is cultivated under irrigation during rabi in regions receiving an average rainfall of 600-800 mm.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In Charotar (Gujarat), bidi tobacco receives 850-900 mm annual rainfall, matures during winter resulting in thick and rugged leaf. In Nipani (Karnataka), it is mostly grown rainfed, and less irrigated crop is prized over more irrigated crop. In Kurnool (Andhra Pradesh), it is rainfed under 670.5 mm annual rainfall (67% SW monsoon, 23% NW monsoon).
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In Uttar Pradesh, climate is semi-arid with ~900 mm rainfall (>70% received June-August; winter showers meagre). Low temperature, low humidity, and bright sunshine during growth are required. Winter crop nurseries are sown in August-September (crop: October-April); summer crop nurseries are sown in February-March (crop: April-June). In Gujarat, rustica tobacco is grown in areas with average annual rainfall of 800 mm.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Lanka tobacco in Andhra Pradesh requires 80 to 90% relative humidity from mid-October to late November with a mean day temperature of about 26.7°C, and requires 30 to 32°C for leaves to mature as temperatures rise.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Light soils produce thin, large-bodied leaves that are light in weight and color, mild in strength, and weak in aroma. Heavy soils produce thick, heavy, dark-colored, strong, and aromatic leaves. In open, light-textured soils, tobacco roots can reach depths of 120 cm. Major soil requirements for maximum leaf expansion are adequate oxygen, water, and plant nutrients.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Ideal soil characteristics for FCV tobacco include: sandy surface soil up to 15–25 cm depth, sandy clay sub-soil up to 150 cm, acidic soil reaction (pH 5.5–6.5), low nutrients and organic matter, very low chloride content, well-drained and aerated soil, with low fertility preferred.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Black soils (Vertisols) used for rainfed rabi FCV tobacco are alkaline, clayey (40-60% clay), high water-holding capacity (70%), high fertility, rich in Ca (4.5-5%) and K, with high CEC saturated with Ca, Mg, K, and Na. Infiltration rate is 0.2 cm/hr and hydraulic conductivity is 0.15 cm/hr, causing slow permeability and risk of oxygen stress/waterlogging. Management interventions include: addition of organic manures, creating field channels along plots for proper drainage, and balanced fertilization/integrated nutrient management.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Northern Light Soils (NLS) derived from sandstones are sandy to sandy loam, moderately acidic, well-drained, low in CEC and water holding capacity, loose, porous, with 20-25% calcium saturation, poor fertility, low fertilizer/water use efficiency, and high leaching. Management interventions include: adequate supply of N, P, K, Ca, and Mg; assured irrigation; and application of organic manures, pond sediments, or mixing of clay to reduce macro-pores, lower hydraulic conductivity, and improve water retention.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Southern Light Soils (SLS) are medium textured red soils, neutral to slightly alkaline, low in organic matter and P, medium to high in K, moderately well drained with moderate to slow permeability. Soil crusting occurs in some red soils. Crusting can be reduced by applying FYM, using soil mulches/plant residue, close growing crops/grasses/legumes, and irrigating to keep soil moist. Other interventions include soil mulching, using a tine cultivator, green manuring, green leaf manuring, soil test-based balanced fertilization, and rainwater harvesting/conjunctive use with ground water.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Karnataka light soils (KLS) range from sandy loams to sandy clay loams, are well drained, dominated by 1:1 clay minerals, slightly acidic, low in inherent fertility, and possess fairly good water-holding capacity. FCV tobacco is cultivated here as a monsoon crop during Kharif.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Chlorides in irrigation water must be < 50 ppm. Irrigating with high chloride water results in saline leaf. Chloride content in the cured leaf must be < 1.5%, as excessive chlorides impair the burning quality of tobacco leaf.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In Agency areas of East and West Godavari (AP), Burley tobacco is grown during monsoon in soils with sandy loam surface and loam sub-soil, pH neutral to acidic (5.5 to 6.5), very low in soluble salts and chlorides, and low in organic matter, available N, and available P. In Vinukonda (Guntur), it is grown rainfed on red gravelly soils poor in soil fertility.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Natu tobacco is grown on medium to heavy black soils with pH 7.0 to 8.5 (poor in available N and organic carbon, medium to high in P, high in available K). It is also cultivated under irrigation on sandy to sandy loam soils with low organic carbon and low available N, P, and K.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Lanka tobacco is cultivated on riverbanks and deltaic islands of Krishna and Godavari rivers on annual flood-deposited alluvial soils ranging from sand to loam. Low-lying silty submerged soils retain abundant moisture and high fertility, allowing repeated yearly cropping. Higher level lands require 2 to 3 irrigations.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In Gujarat, bidi tobacco is grown on sandy to sandy loam soils called 'Goradu' and the Bhatha lands of Mahi and Sabarmati rivers. In Nipani (Karnataka), it is grown on black silt loams with good moisture retention on the banks of Krishna river. In Kurnool (AP), soils range from silt loam to clay where it is raised on conserved moisture.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: In North Bihar, chewing and hookah tobaccos grow in non-saline calcareous sandy loam alluvial soils (pH 7.5 to 8.5) containing up to 45% calcium carbonate, which impedes evaporation and aids water retention, allowing crops to grow without supplemental irrigation. In Tamil Nadu, chewing tobacco is grown in alkaline soils irrigated with high-salt water. In Gujarat, chewing tobacco (Lal Chopadia) is grown in Kaira district.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Motihari (N. rustica) and Jati, wrapper, and filler (N. tabacum) are grown in North Bengal on alluvial flood plain soils of Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers. Soils are less weathered, whitish-grey to greyish sandy loams and silt loams, well-drained and well-aerated, coarse-textured with poor water/nutrient holding capacity, acidic (pH 5.1-6.4), high in available P, and low to medium in available K.
document_name: Soils & Climate

content: Cultivated Tobacco produces long, tubular flowers that are white and rose-colored, whereas Tree Tobacco produces yellow flowers. Blossoms of both species possess 5 long stamens of slightly different lengths and a slender style reaching the corolla tube's mouth. Both produce capsular fruit pods that open to release large numbers of very small seeds.
document_name: Tree Tobacco, NICOTIANA GLAUCA

document_name: Tree Tobacco, NICOTIANA GLAUCA

content: Tree Tobacco is thought to be native to Argentina and has become invasive across the world's warmer regions. It is sometimes cultivated in the Mediterranean region and Iraq because its leaves can be smoked as a stimulant. Medicinally, the leaves have been mashed into a pulp and applied as a poultice to reduce pain and swellings, and to treat bruises, cuts, boils, sores, inflamed throat, and swollen glands.

content: Burley tobacco has a low sugar content, but a high ability to absorb aromas, which is why it is often used in cigarette blends.

content: Oriental tobacco has small leaves and an intense aroma and is grown mainly in Mediterranean regions for specialized tobacco products.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: Archaeological findings of tobacco seeds show that people in North America were using the plant 12,300 years ago.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: Civilizations such as the Mayas and Aztecs incorporated tobacco smoke into religious and ritual practices, often utilizing pipes, while northern Indigenous nations applied tobacco in medical and social rituals. In Native American cultures, tobacco was smoked, chewed, drunk, and snorted as a medium of communication with the supernatural world through shamans. In Mesoamerican societies, it was revered as a divine plant, prepared as liquid infusions or smoked for healing and spiritual rituals.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: Tobacco was introduced to Europe in the late 15th century by European travelers and explorers who brought the plant and usage knowledge. During the 16th century, its use expanded rapidly to Africa and Asia via global trade routes and colonial networks.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: By the 17th and 18th centuries, a widespread smoking culture emerged throughout Europe, making tobacco cultivation economically and socially very significant.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: The Industrial Revolution in the 19th century facilitated the mechanical production of cigarettes and broader tobacco availability. By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, medical literature and scientific research began documenting adverse health effects, linking smoking to respiratory diseases including lung cancer.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: The tobacco market remains large and established, although global raw tobacco production has shown a long-term declining trend. The traditional production base is gradually contracting in many regions under increasing public-health regulation, while tobacco production and trade are becoming relatively more important in several low- and middle-income regions, particularly in Africa.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: China, India, and Brazil were the three largest producers of raw tobacco in 2023, with China producing almost as much as the following nine largest producers combined. Based on 2013–2024 FAOSTAT data, unmanufactured tobacco production was widespread, with China, India, Brazil, and the United States each falling within the highest production class of more than 102,401 t year−1. Production was also substantial across parts of Southeast Asia, South America, and southern and eastern Africa.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: Global trade in raw tobacco reached approximately USD 22.1 billion in 2023. Brazil was the leading exporter of raw tobacco, followed by Zimbabwe, the United States, and India, whereas China remained an important producer, importer, and manufacturer. Trade values for conventional raw and manufactured tobacco products have remained relatively stable over the past decade, while newer categories such as heated tobacco and electronic nicotine-delivery products have shown increasing trade values.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: The biological activity and chemical profile of N. tabacum are largely dominated by alkaloids, particularly nicotine, which serves as the plant's principal defensive compound and major alkaloid accumulated in tobacco leaves.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: The methanolic leaf extract of N. tabacum exhibited significant, dose-dependent antinociceptive (pain-relieving) activity in Wistar mice, increasing pain reaction/latency times and reducing acetic-acid-induced writhing with effects comparable to a standard reference drug.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: In addition to nicotine (present at approximately 10 mg per cigarette), tobacco smoke contains minor alkaloids occurring at microgram-per-cigarette levels, including nornicotine, myosmine, cotinine, anabasine, and anatabine, which interact with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: Tobacco smoke contains terpenes such as limonene and solanesol, which have been linked to neuroprotective and antioxidant properties.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: Tobacco contains bioactive phenolic compounds such as chlorogenic acid and rutin, which are important contributors to its antioxidant capacity.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: The biological effects of tobacco are largely dominated by alkaloids, particularly nicotine, which plays a central role in the plant’s defense mechanisms and its socio-economic impact.

content: Historically, tobacco was used extensively by Indigenous cultures in the Americas as an analgesic, antiseptic, and respiratory aid. Tobacco leaves and infusions were applied topically to wounds, bites, and inflammatory conditions, and smoke was ceremonially used to treat illness or ward off perceived spiritual causes of disease.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: Nicotine is the primary biologically active compound in tobacco responsible for addiction, cardiovascular stimulation, and neurological effects. Processing and consumption, especially smoking, generate harmful substances including tobacco-specific nitrosamines, aldehydes, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: The primary modern medicinal application of tobacco-derived compounds is the controlled administration of nicotine in smoking-cessation products, such as patches, gums, and inhalers, to reduce withdrawal symptoms and dependence on combustible tobacco products.
document_name: Industrial Hemp and Tobacco as Multipurpose Crops: Traditional Uses, Contemporary Applications, and Future Perspectives

content: Nicotine and selected tobacco-derived compounds have been investigated in controlled experimental settings for potential neuroactive and neuroprotective effects, including potential roles in cognitive function and research on neurodegenerative diseases.
